markers.mechanism: Korean -tul plural is extrinsic and spreads across constituents; English -s is local and obligatory after numerals.

examples.input: I bought three apple at the store.
examples.output: I bought three apples at the store.

markers.prompt_hint: Add plural -s to count nouns following numerals greater than one (three apple → three apples, two car → two cars).

markers.mechanism: Korean has no article system; learners default to bare singular nouns where English requires 'a/an' or 'the'.
markers.prompt_hint: Insert 'a', 'an', or 'the' before singular count nouns where the speaker dropped articles.

markers.mechanism: Korean handles psych and causative verbs via bound morphology; learners insert 'to' between English psych verbs and their experiencer.
markers.prompt_hint: Drop superfluous 'to' between psych/causative verbs (shock, surprise, please, anger, frustrate, bore) and the experiencer object.

markers.mechanism: Korean -nun topic marker has no English equivalent; learners calque it as 'as for' fronting structures.

examples.input: As for me, I like apples.

markers.prompt_hint: Drop 'as for X' / 'speaking of X' fronting when the X is the natural subject; preserve only when there is genuine topic contrast.

markers.mechanism: Korean 'uri' (our) is used for individually-possessed things to reflect collectivism (uri anae = 'our wife'); transfer creates anomalous English plurals.

examples.input: I love our wife very much.
examples.output: I love my wife very much.

markers.prompt_hint: Replace plural 'our' with singular 'my' for individually-possessed referents (our wife → my wife, our house → my house) when context shows the speaker is the sole possessor.

markers.mechanism: Korean pragmatics allows context to imply the subject; English requires an overt subject pronoun.

examples.input: Went to the store this morning.
examples.output: I went to the store this morning.

markers.prompt_hint: Restore dropped subject pronouns (typically 'I', 'we', 'they', 'he', 'she') based on context.

markers.mechanism: Korean resultatives use bound morphology; learners avoid English resultative constructions, opting for adverbial workarounds.
markers.prompt_hint: Convert adverbial workarounds (hammered flatly, painted whitely, wiped cleanly) to bare-adjective resultative form (hammered flat, painted white, wiped clean).

markers.mechanism: Korean lexicalizes path morphemes into single verbs; English distributes path across verb + particle ('walk out', 'drive in').

examples.output: He walked out of the room quickly.

markers.prompt_hint: When a single verb encodes path (exited, entered, ascended, descended), expand to manner-verb + particle ('walked out of', 'walked into', 'climbed up') if context indicates a manner of motion.

markers.mechanism: Korean relative clauses precede the head noun (head-final); learners preserve this order in English.

examples.input: The I read book was interesting.
examples.output: The book that I read was interesting.

markers.prompt_hint: Move pre-nominal relative clauses to post-nominal position with 'that' / 'which' / 'who' (the I read book → the book that I read).

notes: Korean typology: Koreanic, SOV, agglutinative, head-final relative clauses, no article system, topic-prominent. Sociolinguistic transfer (collective uri-possessive) is unique among L1 packs. Patterns broadly overlap with Japanese on word order and morphology.
